item.title: Two Ways to Unwittingly Make Your Loved One Feel Worse
item.description:
Stress

Two Ways to Unwittingly Make Your Loved One Feel Worse

Are you taking the wrong approach to calming a loved one in distress?

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • Cognitive reappraisal is usually thought to be the best way to manage stress, but it has its limits.
  • New research suggests that when the stressed-out person isn't you, other approaches may be better.
  • Relationships can benefit when both partners try to bolster each other's stress-busting abilities.

It would seem that one of the key jobs for a good relationship partner is to contribute to that partner’s well-being. However, not everyone is equally skilled at performing this job. Nate’s partner Shelley tends to worry a great deal over little things, often staying up late at night nervously tossing and turning. Ordinarily, Nate can calm Shelley down pretty easily by making a joke or taking on a few more household chores. This time, though, Shelley is inconsolable. It was a bad week at work, and things only seem to be heading in a far worse direction, with possible job loss on the horizon. What can Nate do to help?

The Good and the Bad in Other-Focused Emotion Control

A new study by University of Toronto’s Yitong Zhao and colleagues (2026) adds to the growing body of research on other-focused emotion regulation, in which people try to help those they care about feel better. Shelley, the eternal worrywart, usually manages to figure out how to pull out of an emotional slump. But this time, nothing seems to be working. It would seem that this situation would be a good candidate for Nate to put these other-focused emotion regulation tools into action.

As Zhao et al. point out, the most common way that people try to regulate their own emotions is through cognitive reappraisal, the reframing of a situation so that it doesn’t seem quite so bad. If it was up to Nate and he was feeling this worried, he might tell himself that the job situation could have a silver lining, or that maybe he’s just taking things the wrong way and everything is fine. However, he’s learned that Shelley doesn’t respond to these mental gymnastics, which only seem to make her feel more stressed. What’s worse, Shelley shoots back from these attempts with complaints about Nate’s apparent lack of empathy.

The problem here is that, in the words of the authors, “managing a recipient’s emotions may introduce unique challenges, given that regulation may not match the recipients’ preferences and good intentions may get lost in translation” (p. 1508). Reappraisal runs the risk of invalidating the recipient’s emotions. This falls into the general category of backfiring when you try to change a loved one’s personality or behaviors. Rather than say that the person you love is wrong, flawed, or misinterpreting situations, what’s called “decommitment,” you instead should use “commitment” strategies in which you don’t question but instead support the other person’s interpretation. From there, you can suggest ways to manage the emotion in ways that don’t make the stressed-out person feel invalidated.

Testing Decommitment vs. Commitment in Other-Focused Emotion Control

Across three studies spanning different approaches, Zhao et al. compared commitment with decommitment strategies of other-focused emotion control on outcomes that included relationship quality of well-being of the partner. The samples included demographically diverse online and community samples.

The comparison of emotion control strategies included these two basic demarcations:

Decommitment tactics: Reducing severity (“It is not that bad”) and situational acceptance (“It’s out of your hands”)

Commitment tactics: Enhancing controllability (“you can handle it”) and findings benefits (“it will make you stronger”).

The findings consistently supported the benefits of commitment vs. decommitment tactics. Challenging a partner’s interpretations either made things worse or had no appreciable positive impact. Commitment strategies, in contrast, were associated with better outcomes. The key attribute of the commitment strategy, they conclude, is that it helps your partner “generate a novel framework” (p. 1523). It all comes down to helping a stressed love one switch goals rather than switch the way the situation is perceived.

Turning Decommitment into Commitment Strategies

It can be very tempting to use the tried-and-true cognitive reappraisal mantra that’s so generally accepted in the fields of stress, anxiety, and depression. Stress may be, as is often said, “in the mind of the beholder,” but if the mind is someone else’s, not yours, a challenging reappraisal can make that other person feel not only misunderstood, but inadequate.

The simplicity of the commitment strategies makes the findings from the U. Toronto study even more impressive. Reinforcing your loved one's psychological strength can be a matter of uttering just a few simple, if not obvious, words of encouragement. However, the authors do go on to suggest some deeper and perhaps less obvious reasons for why this all should work.

One is that through this strategy, you communicate that you want to help, not judge. Second, you show that you are willing to do what's needed to ease the other person's stress. Does your loved one want you to be a sounding board? Or might you be needed to validate the fact that the situation actually is as bad as the other person thinks it is? In the example of Nate and Shelley, by letting Shelley know that the work thing actually is a problem would be more effective than if Nate dismissed Shelley’s response as usual over-the-top worrying over inconsequential problems.

Another benefit of commitment strategies is that they support the other person’s sense of competence. The stress literature is clear that one major source of stress is the belief that the challenge you face is greater than your ability to handle it. Bolster your sense of competence, and the challenge may fade in proportion.

To sum up, when stress reduction is a two-person process, it’s important to take the other person's perspective. Rather than hear your supposedly “logical” counter-position, the person you love will benefit more from hearing that the stress is real, and so is your loved one’s ability to handle it.

item.title: Healthy Phone Practices for Teens and Tweens
item.description:
Parenting

Healthy Phone Practices for Teens and Tweens

How parents can plan for and guide their children's entry into smartphones.

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • Phone use is often a point of contention in families.
  • Parents frequently use age rather than maturity as the top consideration in getting that first phone.
  • Phone removal is overused as a punishment for teens and tweens.

In our current world, the question isn’t whether a child will get a cell phone. It is instead when to get one and how to support the healthy use of such a powerful device. Despite the prevalence of cell phones in the lives of families, we have yet to hear a caregiver say, “My children aren’t on their screens enough.” This edited excerpt from our book, Working with Parents in Child Psychotherapy, is focused on helping parents guide their children in cell phone use.

In the early days of our psychology careers, before the advent of smartphones, parents used to ask us if they should put a television in their child’s room. Our answer was typically no, because having their own TV would interfere with the child’s sleep and be more isolating than watching a show in a common family area. Now nearly every child, by virtue of having a phone, tablet, or laptop, can have a TV in their room, and caregivers don’t even ask this question anymore!

In thinking about how to adopt healthy phone practices, we suggest considering carefully some of the common issues that arise:

1. Caregivers have often promised that a child will receive a phone at a certain time point. Most children want a personal device. That said, rather than setting that specific time in advance, we suggest that the parents consider when it would be a benefit for this child to attain a phone. The general sensibility is to get a device around middle school, either at the start of sixth grade or in eighth grade when one is graduating and approaching high school. We argue that readiness should not be based on a given age but instead on individual considerations such as maturity, ability to care for expensive items, management of other screen time, including stopping when asked, and interest and ability in being engaged in other nonscreen activities. The following questions can also help you consider the timing of getting a child their own phone:

  • What will the child do on their phone?
  • Can the child achieve what they wish or need on a shared family device?
  • Will the phone help caregivers stay in touch with or track their child when they are engaged in independent activities?
  • What is the likely impact of having a phone on the child’s friendships? For example, will it enable friendships if friends are already primarily communicating by text or other social media? Or will it impede friendships if the child finds the phone more attractive than interacting with friends?
  • Is the child likely to become distressed by content on their phone?

2. Parents should develop clear expectations for phone use ahead of time. When giving a child a phone, start with more rules and then, over time, let them have more freedom rather than vice versa. Rules can include charging the phone in the caregivers’ room or in a neutral location at a specific time each night. Another useful expectation involves requiring that caregivers have the passwords to access the child’s accounts. The American Academy of Pediatrics (2021) offers a guide to creating a family media plan, which helps the family come to shared agreements about device use. Rules can be reevaluated based on issues such as how the rules are working given the child’s developmental level, social context, and family situation.

3. Develop expectations for phone-free time. What is lost by having a phone? What are the effects on sleeping, hobbies, and family interactions? Spending time in bed with a phone at night can have detrimental effects on children’s sleep, as can waking up extra early to engage in device use. Non-device-related activities and hobbies should continue, rather than being traded in for game time on a phone. In general, parents can model the ability to stop using a device, especially during mealtimes. Many parents, for example, are sometimes unable to charge their phones outside their room or take a break from their own screens to interact with their children.

4. Avoid the overuse of phone removal as a penalty, especially for behaviors unrelated to phone use. For some families, minimizing the conflict around how much screen time children are allowed may include reducing the use of phone removal as the go-to punishment. These types of penalties only make phone use more desirable. It has been amazing to see the number of hacks kids have come up with to avoid penalties around losing access to devices and apps. However, if the reason parents want to remove the phone is due to misbehavior related to its use, reducing, removing, or altering access may be justified.

5. Once you get your children phones, pay attention to what they are doing on them. Be familiar with the shows, games, and people children engage with on their phones. We recommend erring on the side of limiting access to content, especially when it is not age-appropriate, especially for anxious or depressed children.

Getting a child their first phone is often a rite of passage in many families. Be sure to plan ahead and think carefully to make it a positive decision.

item.title: The Key to the Lindsay Clancy Case: Defining Psychosis
item.description:
Psychosis

The Key to the Lindsay Clancy Case: Defining Psychosis

Was it postpartum depression or postpartum psychosis?

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • Psychosis is still a mysterious and enigmatic phenomenon.
  • There is more than one way to conceptualize psychosis.
  • How we comprehend psychosis informs the way we treat it.

This is Part 3 of a series on the controversial Lindsay Clancy case. Read Part 2 here.

Source: Ken Lund/CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons

The crucial question of whether Lindsay Clancy was or was not psychotic at the time of the crime was central to the recent mistrial. Apparently, 11 of the 12 jurors were convinced that she lacked criminal responsibility for her actions. But was this because they believed Clancy had been suffering from postpartum psychosis or only severe postpartum depression?

One of the primary problems with the differential diagnosis and conveying it to the jurors is related to the still extremely poor understanding, both in psychiatry and psychology and the general public, of the fundamental nature of psychosis. What is psychosis? What causes it? What is its significance? And who is really at risk for developing it?

What Is Psychosis?

Psychosis is a very broad category of mental disorder with a relatively vague definition. But most mental health professionals today would agree that psychosis basically consists of the presence of hallucinations and/or delusions, usually marked impairment that grossly interferes with social, occupational, or day-to-day functioning, and deficient "reality testing" or a so-called "break with reality." Schizophrenia, which appears in approximately 0.5 percent to 1.5 percent of the population across cultures, is one classic form of psychosis. But there are several other kinds of psychotic disorders specified in the DSM 5-TR, including unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders, schizophreniform disorder, schizoaffective disorder, brief psychotic disorder, delusional disorder, shared psychotic disorder, substance-induced psychotic disorder, and psychotic disorder due to a general medical condition. In addition, psychosis may be experienced by sufferers of severe major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, or borderline, paranoid, and schizotypal personality disorder when under stress. And although psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia are chronically debilitating, some, like delusional disorder, are less so as regards daily functioning.

Conceptualizing Psychosis

Most psychiatrists and clinical psychologists today take an almost exclusively biological, medicalized view of psychosis, believing it to be a "broken brain" disease. A "mental illness." A genetically inherited neurobiological abnormality. A fundamentally physiological phenomenon. But this is merely one still unproven theory of psychosis. Indeed, there may be somewhat different etiologies for different psychotic disorders, different courses of the illness, and different prognoses. The statistical fact is that multiple studies of identical twins have shown concordance rates (meaning the probability that both monozygotic twins will be schizophrenic) ranging from around 35 percent to 70 percent, indicating a significant (average of about 50 percent) but only partial, not total (or 100 percent), genetic basis for psychosis.

In my book Anger, Madness, and the Daimonic (1996), I present some alternative ways of conceptualizing psychosis (what we historically call madness) and discuss its close connection to repressed anger or rage in particular, and, more generally, a long-standing repression, dissociation, or denial of the daimonic (see May, 1969; Diamond, 1996, 2026). For example, the relatively rare phenomenon known as folie à deux, shared psychotic disorder, or induced delusional disorder in which one dependent person adopts the psychotic worldview of another more dominant individual, clearly illustrates the psychological rather than neurobiological causes of psychosis in certain cases. (Indeed, some studies have shown that schizophrenic patients have a significantly higher history of childhood trauma than the general population, which begs the question of whether their illness could be trauma-based.)

Another way of conceptualizing psychosis is that it is a stress-induced existential crisis involving an acute distortion of reality due to finding consensual reality as it is unacceptable or intolerable. (This linkage of psychosis with stress is supported by the classic diathesis-stress model, which posits an interaction between genetic predisposition and environmental stressors.) Psychosis can also be seen at least partly as an elaborately constructed and carefully maintained unconscious psychological defense mechanism guarding against intimacy and fending off existential reality so as to avoid being abandoned, rejected, disappointed, or otherwise retraumatized.

How one conceptualizes psychosis, or any other mental disorder, dictates and informs how we go about trying to treat that condition. (Only a few centuries ago, psychosis, madness, or insanity was believed to be caused by demonic possession, for which exorcism was considered the only remedy, and there are still those today who believe themselves to be possessed and seek out exorcism when conventional psychiatric treatment seems insufficient.) How we conceptualize psychosis also affects the capacity to understand the risks or vulnerabilities in particular individuals for becoming psychotic at some point in their lives. (For example, consider the DSM-5-TR proposed diagnosis of attenuated psychosis syndrome, previously psychosis risk syndrome in DSM-5, a condition defined by the presence of mild psychotic-like symptoms with relatively intact reality testing that, while not severe enough to be diagnosed as psychosis, can, in 15 percent to 35 percent of cases, be prodromal to developing a true psychotic disorder within several years.)

Indeed, even the great psychiatrist C.G. Jung, a pioneer in the psychotherapeutic treatment of psychosis, seems to have experienced some psychotic symptoms triggered by the psychosocial stressors of being excommunicated by Freud and the Freudians, precipitating a profound midlife crisis persisting for more than a decade. He conceptualized and characterized his own personal experience (Jung, 1961, 2009) as an encounter or "confrontation with the unconscious," which he courageously and consciously elected to submit to, deeply explore, and document, and, as a result, was eventually transformed by this terrifying experience. (See my prior post.) Indeed, much of what he later came to call "analytical psychology" derived from this extraordinary, prolonged, perilous, and disorienting inner odyssey. Thus, from a Jungian perspective, psychosis is the consequence of being inundated, overwhelmed, overrun, or possessed by the unconscious and its complexes and, as a result, becoming confused between inner and outer reality.

Having said all that, I submit that no one, even the most "normal" person, is completely immune to experiencing psychosis or, at least, psychotic symptoms. Psychosis is a deeply disturbing and distressing state of mind that any of us can succumb to under the right or wrong circumstances. I understand that this is both a controversial and frightening assertion. We prefer to think of psychosis as something that happens only to other less fortunate, genetically vulnerable individuals. But this is not true. And if, as I suggest, we all possess the congenital capacity or potentiality for psychosis, transitory or otherwise, i.e., if psychosis is an archetypal human experience, would this indicate that we all carry within us the genetic predisposition for it? Is psychosis rooted in what Jung (1961) called an "archetype," an "inherited structure of the psyche," a pre-existing, innate, potential form or pattern of human behavior or experience present in every person?

Conclusion

Did Lindsay Clancy truly suffer from postpartum psychosis or merely severe postpartum depression without psychotic symptoms, both of which are triggered or exacerbated by the biopsychosocial stressors of giving birth? Was the defendant really experiencing auditory command hallucinations and paranoid delusions of thought broadcasting at or just prior to the commission of the crime? If so, she was, by any definition, psychotic and, in the eyes of the law, not sane or responsible. Or, more cynically, could Ms. Clancy have been malingering (something that occurs in an estimated 8 percent to 21 percent of forensic cases such as this) by intentionally mentioning those symptoms, perhaps drawing upon her professional experience as a registered labor and delivery nurse to manipulate others into believing she was psychotic at that time? On that key question, the jury is still out.

item.title: Medical First Responders: Unsung Heroes
item.description:
Disaster Psychology

Medical First Responders: Unsung Heroes

Recognizing the heroism of health care first responders benefits everyone.

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • The term hero applies to health care first responders, but their heroic acts are less likely to be recognized.
  • Health care first responders are at risk for long-term threats of disease and mental health challenges.
  • Devoted to alleviating suffering, medical responders risk suffering vicariously with those they help.
  • Recognizing their heroic efforts can enhance recruitment to and support for their life-sustaining profession.
Source: Krystine I. Batcho

Most often when we hear references to heroes, we think of soldiers, firefighters, or law enforcement. Dictionary entries for “heroism” are typically circular, defining heroism in terms of the qualities of a hero or heroic conduct. The most common synonym for heroism is courage, and a hero is described as a person with special abilities or personal heroic qualities.

In crises that range from immense to limited, among those near the frontline of responders are medical professionals, willing to risk their lives to rescue and save others. Sharing the common attribute of courage with those who are trained to fight and/or overcome physical obstacles and danger, medical first responders are distinguished by their primary goal to preserve life and prepare the ill and injured for healing, recovery, and restoration to health.

So, why are nonmedical responders more often recognized as heroes and medical professionals seemingly overlooked? Perhaps medical professionals are thought of as second-line responders. The underlying logic dictates that threats and obstacles must be overcome before medical care can be administered. Lifesaving efforts are ideally carried out in areas of safety. The media present the most dramatic images of extreme incidents of natural disasters, horrific bridge and building collapses, wildfires, mass shootings, and war. Prominent in such scenes are responders in uniform, while physicians and health care professionals are unseen or in the background.

However, over the last 20 years, responses to disaster and mass casualty events have benefited from lessons learned from battleground trauma, mass shootings, attacks with explosive devices, plane crashes, and other crises. Collaborative efforts applying lifesaving measures at the scene have improved survival rates and show promise for continuing increases in positive outcomes. Despite the increasing presence and involvement of emergency medical professionals in disaster and crisis events, society remains less likely to recognize physicians as heroes than it does firefighters and law enforcement.

The dangers medical providers face with courage and altruistic service are often invisible. During the pandemic, medical first responders risked death from COVID-19, and during mass casualty events, they are exposed to unknown contagion, exposure to toxins, and violence. Courage is often defined as heroic action despite feelings of intense fear. The psychological burden courageous medical first responders bear is evident in their heightened exposure to prolonged stress. The prevalence of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is significantly higher among emergency medicine providers compared to other health care professionals and the general population. Medical responders are also at risk for other mental health challenges, including depression, and mourning the loss of coworkers and victims. Attracted and dedicated to their profession’s mission to alleviate suffering and promote wellness, medical providers are acutely vulnerable to suffering vicariously with patients and victims. The deeper their compassion and the more astute their empathy, the more intensely they suffer.

Heroic acts are typically understood to be those done to save or protect the lives of others, and heroes are those who accept risks to their own safety or health for the well-being of others. By such standards, medical first responders are heroes. More often than not, they remain unsung heroes, overshadowed by heroes who carry more imposing tools and weapons to combat highly graphic, life-threatening perils of fire, explosions, gunfire, and structural collapse. They don’t ask for recognition, but in our time dominated by enhanced imagery, acknowledging their heroic service could benefit society by increasing support for and recruitment to a demanding but noble profession.

item.title: The Future of Football
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

The Future of Football

Will football be with us for good?

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • 150 million Americans follow football, a popular, dangerous game.
  • Alarming new evidence links professional football and brain injury.
  • Popularity does not guarantee persistence.

Three quarters of a century ago, the preeminent cultural historian Jacques Barzun wrote, “Whoever wants to know the heart and mind of America had better learn baseball.”

Baseball favors a measured, pastoral rhythm, Barzun wrote. Baseball has a democratic cast, requiring every player to come to bat, even pitchers who usually are not very good at it. Much is left to chance in baseball, and this keeps Americans who like taking chances on the edges of their seats. There is no game clock in baseball. Baseball leaves fans and spectators time for conversation. Baseball’s rules provide checks and balances. Placing the mound out 90 feet evens the odds between batter and pitcher. A bit like the United States Constitution balances governance, Barzun thought. So the game fit the country. That was then.

A lot of water has flowed under the bridge since 1954, and baseball, once key to understanding the currents of our character and our psychology, has slipped to a distant third in popularity. Basketball has climbed past baseball to the number two slot, with about one and a half million watching a game on television. But a single regular season football game now attracts 20 or 25 million American viewers, and that adds up to about 150 million football fans in the United States. It’s no contest.

Baseball, played in a park, tuned to slow, summer, rural rhythms when a third of Americans still lived on farms. Football fits a corporate, urbanized, keyed-up America. Football plays out in bursts of rigidly timed intervals. Football is minutely planned and efficiently managed. Artificial intelligence now sits alongside assistant coaches, helping them crunch data in the booth high above the field. Football makes players specialists not just in their roles in the game, but in their very bodies. (No one, even from a distance, will mistake an offensive tackle for a sleek defensive safety.) Where baseball is leisurely, football is explosive and best understood among the predatory sports, Barzun thought. Football requires violent physical contact on every play.

Chuck Klosterman, a sports essayist, has written a wry and intelligent meditation simply titled Football. He offered an audacious prediction. In another six or seven decades, he believes, football will have gone the way of fencing, horseracing, and boxing. Culture changes. Sports come and go.

We no longer routinely carry swords, and so fencing is niche as niche can be. Hundreds of thousands of horses once traveled American city streets. So we loved watching them race. And boxing was once a manly rite of passage; we took our lumps and gave them. Prizefighting, the pinnacle of that spirit, now festers with brain injury and corruption, living mostly in pay-per-view. Mixed martial arts satisfy bloodlust for some.

Collision Is the Name of the Game

On the eve of the season opener here in my football-involved hometown, I tested the notion of the game’s eventual eclipse on several fans, fellow panting gym rats. This question invited a chorus of derision. The consensus? No way. But when inquiring about the epidemic of CTE (chronic traumatic encephalopathy) among famous NFL players—Frank Gifford, Junior Seau, Ken Stabler, Brett Favre, perhaps Jason Kelce, so he believes—the confident opinion faltered.

One mother didn’t mind me asking a follow-up about her son, an enthusiastic hockey-playing third grader, what she would say the day he asked for permission to play football. Hockey has its own injury profile, she acknowledged, but football raised special concern for her because the toll of playing football is cumulative. (She has a medical background.) She pointed out that it is not just the concussion that knocks players silly that bodes ill; it is the micro-concussion of routine collision that adds up. And collision, as the TV commentator might say, is the name of the game.

But Football Fosters Fortitude

It is easy to list the virtues of the game. Football depends upon teamwork, as every player has a vital task, even the unexalted linemen who make the big plays possible. (I watch the front line with special care in the weekly contests, having played the line both on offense and defense back in the late Paleolithic.) But bolstering fortitude may be chief among the bonuses of playing football.

Football is not for the unresilient. Football players learn to huddle up and bounce back. And further, playing football entails steeling oneself to pain, a kind of bravery that eludes us in our comfortable, protected lives now. Football teaches a player to shake it off. That lesson proves close to invaluable. How else can we learn it?

Millions held their breaths while on-field physicians revived Buffalo Bills defensive safety Damar Hamlin.
Source: Mural by Adam Zyglis, photo courtesy Jessica Zyglis (2023)

But…

But the compounding effects of cumulative impact that accompany blocking and tackling almost certainly cannot be shaken off in the long run. Football is dangerous. The bad effects linger. The longer players play, the worse the effects.

The clinical picture has sharpened since I wrote about it four seasons ago. The most alarming study, released this August, found that of those former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 who had arranged to have their brains autopsied, 91.4 percent tested positive for CTE.

So, what are we to do with such an alarming finding? Protective equipment might be improved to the point where players are padded like the Michelin Man. Klosterman poses the pointed question, “Why has society coalesced around a sport that wrecks people’s brains?” We like the strategies and marvel at the skills, of course. But his answer is subtler. Though football is not a blood sport like boxing, it is still the near prospect of the devastating hit that makes the spectator sport compelling.

The Future

So. Should football be banned? Nonsense. It is hard to imagine Ohio in fall without football. The same can be said for Michigan, Nebraska, Texas, and Florida. We are conditioned to assume that popularity entails permanence. Klosterman envisions our current life as the future’s history.

And that makes it easier to picture that the millions of individual family decisions over the next three generations will begin to starve football of talent and allure. Those mothers and fathers who steer their high school kids to safer sports will shrink the pool of gifted recruits. When college football—the feeder system—eventually dwindles, the professional game will soon shrivel.

In that projection, football will end not with a ban, but with bare, emptied stadiums.

The mother of the young hockey player got a laugh from the group with a further speculation. By the year 2100, she predicted, not implausibly, sentient robots would be playing the game. “And they wouldn’t need helmets.” But that is the crux, isn’t it?

item.title: 'Musterbation' Makes Us Miserable
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

'Musterbation' Makes Us Miserable

Don't allow musts to live rent-free in your brain.

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • What we tell ourselves under our breath can have profound effects on our emotional states.
  • One word that can bring the hammer down on your feelings about yourself is the word “must.”
  • 'Musterbation' is a form of thinking that can make you miserable.
Source: Ekaterina Belinskaya/Pexels

Readers who follow this blog may know that it often highlights the power of words and how they impact us. A change in one word can make a big difference, as a suitor may find out when they pop the question and get a “no” in response.

In practicing cognitive behavioral therapy, I've learned to pay close attention to the particular words patients use when they speak about themselves and their life experiences. No big reveal here, but I’ve noticed that helping them tweak their inner speech can have positive effects on their emotional states.

Changing a word here and there may not seem like much. But if you regularly monitor what you say to yourself under your breath and switch a word here and there, you may be surprised at how such a little change can affect how you feel. The focus here is on one of the most troublesome little words that can bring the hammer down on our emotional well-being—the word “must.” There are many situations in which “must” words matter, such as when we say to ourselves, “I must do this," "I must achieve that,” or its inverse, "I mustn't do that."

The Tyranny of the Must

The word "must" derives from Old English roots meaning “to have to.” It is an imperative that dictates what we are required to do. Musts enter our vocabulary early in life when parents issue commands such as, “You must brush your teeth," or "You mustn't hit other children." We are told what we must or mustn’t do and that we will suffer the consequences of violating these demands. Children also encounter musts in the context of religious or moral training, as when they learn about Biblical injunctions and commandments. The must is a lever used to socialize children to follow social rules, parental expectations, and moral teachings.

We may become so entrenched in the language of musts and its cousins in crime, shoulds, ought-to’s, and have-to’s, that as adults we hold ourselves to absolutist standards and expectations that brook no exceptions. If we find ourselves or the world writ large falling short of meeting these internalized commandments, we may dump on ourselves or adopt a dour outlook on life in general. Here is a sampling of musts I hear from my patients:

  • I must be more successful than my younger brothers.
  • I must be married before my 30th birthday.
  • I must succeed in everything I do.
  • I must get approval from everyone I meet.
  • I mustn’t make anyone angry with me.
  • I mustn’t get angry at someone else.
  • I must make every day count, and if I don’t, I’m a failure.

What are the musts knocking around in your head? Why are you letting them live rent-free in your brain?

'Musterbation' Is Harmful

The psychologist Albert Ellis famously challenged the tyranny of musts and shoulds, pointing out that many people make themselves miserable by imposing insistent demands on themselves, believing they must be competent in everything they do, always succeed or else, be loved and accepted by everyone, and never risk another person’s disapproval. Somewhat tongue-in-cheek, he referred to this practice as musterbation, which can have pernicious effects on our emotional well-being and cause emotional distress.

Ellis encouraged people to replace musts with more flexible preferences. For example, the belief, “I must be competent in everything I do," can be replaced with a more flexible thought: “I want to succeed and would prefer to succeed, but I don’t have to succeed at everything I do.” In the first case, a rigidly held must can lead to a sense of personal failure when you fall short of a demand. In the second case, a failure or setback may be unfortunate, but it does not make you a failure as a person. We may want others to like us, but we can tolerate their disapproval. Tying self-worth to other people’s approval makes it dependent on the actions of others—actions we cannot directly control.

"I Must Have Your Approval, or Else!"

A common form of musterbation is believing you must at all times have the approval of everyone important to you, and that the risk of displeasing other people is the psychological equivalent of falling off the edge of the planet. One of my patients had spent his entire life as a people-pleaser. He was the dutiful and obedient son, the good student, the friend who would sacrifice anything for the other person. Throughout his life, he was the one person everyone could count on to take care of their needs—everyone’s needs, except his own. He had never allowed himself to recognize, let alone express his own needs, feelings, wants, or desires out of fear of garnering disapproval. In the course of therapy, he began to question the musts of people-pleasing and of merely living as a reflection of what other people expected him to be.

The tyranny of people-pleasing has been recognized since antiquity. As readers of this blog may know, I often draw upon the wisdom of an ancient Stoic philosopher whose day job happened to be running the Roman Empire. He was the philosopher and Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius (121 – 180 A.D.), whose thoughts and reflections are compiled in his Meditations, which is widely considered to be among the classics of Western Civilization. In one passage, Marcus reminds us of an obvious contradiction—at least obvious when we lay it out logically—of putting the opinions of others above our own. As Marcus wrote, "It never ceases to amaze me: we all love ourselves more than other people, but care more about their opinion than our own."

If you are concerned about your emotional well-being or experiencing any significant mental health problems, I encourage you to consult a licensed mental health professional in your area for a thorough evaluation.

item.title: Why a 10-Minute "Very Slow Jog" Boosts Mood and Brain Power
item.description:
Happiness

Why a 10-Minute "Very Slow Jog" Boosts Mood and Brain Power

A walking-pace jog improves prefrontal cortex function and boosts happiness.

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • A brief 10-minute bout of very slow running significantly enhances positive mood and executive function.
  • The "head bobbing" unique to running may stimulate brain regions that release serotonin.
  • Unlike heel-strike walking, the airborne mechanics of a slow jog create distinct cognitive benefits.
Source: Vitalii Petrenko / Shutterstock

Accumulating evidence suggests that hitting 10,000 steps a day isn't the only way to unlock the health benefits of daily movement. Three recent 2026 studies show that slightly increasing your gait speed or walking continuously for 13 to 36 minutes significantly lowers both mortality and dementia risk.

But if you're looking for an immediate mood boost and prefrontal cortex activation, you might want to change your biomechanics rather than your pace. Another new 2026 study found that keeping your speed exactly the same—but picking up your feet to break into a super-slow, 10-minute jog—rapidly increases happiness and enhances executive function.

The Neuroscience of a Super-Slow Jog

A wealth of science links cardiovascular exercise to better cognitive and mental health. However, researchers are increasingly interested in the absolute minimum dose of exercise—in terms of intensity, duration, and frequency—required to trigger neurological benefits.

The latest (2026) "slow running benefits" study published in Imaging Neuroscience set out to find the minimum intensity threshold for running needed to improve mood and prefrontal cognition. Led by Hideaki Soya at the University of Tsukuba, researchers had 24 healthy adults complete a 10-minute "super-slow" running session on a treadmill.

For this study, the pace was dialed down to roughly 2.9 to 3.5 mph (a 17- to 21-minute-per-mile pace)—speeds you could easily maintain at a brisk walk, just below the 4.0 mph threshold where most people naturally transition from a walk to a jog.

Before and after the session, participants completed a Stroop task (a classic measure of executive function) and a mood questionnaire while wearing functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) caps to monitor cortical blood flow.

The results were immediate and striking. Just 10 minutes of glacially slow running significantly reduced Stroop interference time and elicited left lateral prefrontal cortex (PFC) activation. Participants also reported feeling noticeably more cheerful.

The Biomechanics of Head Bobbing

If you can walk at the exact same speed, why does jogging trigger such a distinct neurological response? The answer lies in the unique biomechanics of how we move through space.

Technically, running differs from walking by being partially airborne. When you walk, one foot is always in contact with the earth. When you run—even at a snail's pace—both feet leave the ground for a fraction of a second. This bounces you through each stride, creating a rhythmic vertical oscillation.

Soya and his colleagues attached sensors to the participants' skulls to measure how much their bobbing heads rose and fell with each step. They discovered a significant positive correlation between the magnitude of this head acceleration and the participants' pleasant mood.

In animal models, this specific vertical bouncing activates neurons that release serotonin, a neurotransmitter heavily linked to mood regulation. Interestingly, head acceleration or "bobbing" is nominal during walking and virtually nonexistent when cycling.

Evolutionary Trade-Offs: Walking vs. Running

To fully appreciate why a slow jog feels so different to the brain, it helps to look at the evolutionary biomechanics of hominin bipedalism. A September 2026 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) analyzed the detailed 3D kinematics of how humans walk compared to our closest living relatives, chimpanzees.

The researchers found that human walking is defined by a consistent heel-strike, a trait chimpanzees rarely use. This evolutionary adaptation allows modern humans to save an estimated 26 to 41 percent of metabolic energy compared to walking on the ball of the foot. By rolling smoothly from the heel to the front of the foot, we evolved to walk vast distances with incredible metabolic efficiency, though it comes at the cost of higher impact forces on our joints.

But this metabolic efficiency is exactly why breaking into a jog changes the neurobiological equation. When you transition from an energy-saving heel-strike walk into a bouncy, airborne jog—often shifting toward a midfoot strike—you recruit different muscle groups and alter the mechanical stress on your body. The cerebellum's Purkinje cells must rapidly adjust their prediction models to maintain balance and coordinate the complex timing of landing and pushing off.

The slight increase in physiological demand, combined with the rhythmic vertical oscillation of your skull, sends a completely different sensory payload to your brain. You are no longer just transporting yourself efficiently; you're dynamically challenging your nervous system.

Putting This Research Into Practice

You don't need to be an elite ultra-endurance athlete or push your heart rate to the absolute limit to reap the cognitive rewards of running.

  • Peak Performance Primer: Just before a demanding mental task, presentation, test, or high-stakes call, try a 10-minute slow jog around the block or up and down a long hallway.
  • Keep It Conversational: Dial the intensity down to a pace where you can easily hold a conversation. The goal isn't cardiovascular exhaustion; it's rhythmic movement.
  • Focus on the Bounce: Allow your body to naturally oscillate up and down. You don't need a heavy, pounding stride. A light, springy, short-stepped jog is enough to trigger the head acceleration your brain thrives on.

If 10,000 steps or high-intensity intervals feel like too much of a hurdle today, give yourself permission to go slow. A 10-minute jog at a walking pace can instantly boost your mood and promote better prefrontal cortex function.

item.title: The Hidden Burden of Being Loved Too Much
item.description:
Relationships

The Hidden Burden of Being Loved Too Much

4 reasons why you may want to be loved less.

Posted September 12, 2026

Key points
  • The healthiest romantic love is not about being loved less, but about being loved more adequately.
  • Love involves not only closeness but also freedom, autonomy, and individual identity.
  • Being seen with our imperfections may be more valuable than being idealized.
  • We may appreciate being deeply important to someone without wanting to become their entire universe.

Most people dream of being loved more. But can people also feel they are loved too much? Is the notion of “too much love” plausible? I believe it is. The wish to be loved less often arise from four major characteristics of romantic love: (1) love as fusion, (2) the idealizing nature of love, (3) the partial nature of love, and (4) the intense nature of romantic love. In each case, more love does not necessarily mean better love.

1. Love as Fusion

“Erotic love is the craving for complete fusion, for union with one other person.” — Erich Fromm

Romantic love is often portrayed as the fusion of two individuals into a single entity. But fusion implies not only closeness; it can also threaten freedom, autonomy, and individual identity. Love should ideally provide conditions for personal growth and self-development—goals that can conflict with the ideal of fusion (Ben-Ze’ev, 2019).

When love is understood as fusion, people may actually wish their partner loved them somewhat less, while preserving a significant degree of freedom for both partners. Romantic relationships are better understood as forms of functional harmony rather than literal fusion: two independent individuals coordinating their lives without becoming a single person. Profound love therefore does not require eliminating all distance between partners. Indeed, some distance enables each person to remain a distinct and flourishing individual.

2. The Idealizing Nature of Love

“I am a firm believer in moderation. Yet I don't think there is moderation in love.” — Rosa

Too much Love
Source: pexels-viridianaor-29567547

Love is often understood in highly idealized terms, both regarding the beloved and the expected durability of the relationship. Lovers are encouraged to devote themselves to the other’s happiness, and place their own needs in the background. They may also become blind to significant flaws, constructing an overly idealized image of the person they love.

In this view, love leaves little room for compromise or accommodation, because love conquers all and sets us on fire. Likewise, there can be no limits, as expressed in the familiar romantic claim that there is “no mountain high enough” to stop one’s love. An undistorted picture of reality is important for navigating the world, but positive illusions can sometimes benefit romantic relationships. Yet their value is usually greatest when they remain moderate.

Excessive idealization creates expectations that no real person or relationship can sustain. Hence, people may wish their partner would idealize them less and see them more realistically. Being loved by someone who recognizes our imperfections may be more valuable than being adored by someone who sees only an idealized version of us (Ben-Ze'ev & Goussinsky, 2008).

3. The Partial Nature of Love

“When a man loves a woman, he can’t keep his mind on nothing else.” — Percy Sledge

Emotions are partial in two senses. First, they are cognitively partial because they focus attention on a limited target, often one person or a small number of people. Second, they are evaluatively partial because they express a personal and interested perspective. Romantic love directs and shapes our attention by selecting what attracts and holds it. As romantic love focuses resources on a particular person, that person seems overwhelmingly important. Yet being the exclusive focus of another person can become burdensome. A beloved may occasionally wish to step out of the spotlight—to be less intensely observed, less constantly desired, and less central to another person’s life.

In this sense, being loved less can mean having more personal space. We may appreciate being deeply important to someone without wanting to become their entire universe.

4. The Intense Nature of Romantic Love

“When you put your arms around me, I get a fever that’s so hard to bear.”—Peggy Lee
Romantic love is often marked by intense emotional arousal, especially in its early stages, before we adapt to the experience. Romantic love is like a laser beam: the narrower the beam, the greater its intensity. Intensity brings urgency, emotional heat, and heightened attention. Under such circumstances, even minor concerns can acquire extraordinary significance. This helps explain why telling someone, “I love you a little,” or even “I love you moderately,” sounds insulting. Such statements may express affection, but they fail to convey the intensity that romantic love is expected to have.

Yet intensity is neither always sustainable nor always desirable. A relationship in which every emotion is amplified can become exhausting. Constant passion may leave little room for calmness, patience, reflection, or independent pursuits. The paradox is that what feels wonderful in limited doses may become burdensome when experienced continuously.

Love Me Less and Let Me Live More Adequately

“Love is all you need.” — The Beatles

Many people suffer from not being loved enough. Far fewer reflect on the costs of being loved excessively. Although coping with too much love may be easier than coping with too little, it can still impose various burdens. Fusion can threaten autonomy; idealization can distance us from reality; partiality can make us the excessive focus of another person; and intensity can transform ordinary aspects of life into emotionally charged events. However, none of this suggests that we should seek distant detached relationships. Rather, it reminds us that more love is not always better love (here).

Healthy romantic relationships leave room for growth. Intrinsic activities are essential to a flourishing life, and an important role of a romantic partner is to support, rather than replace, personal fulfillment. We need shared experiences with our partners, but we also need opportunities to pursue activities that are distinctly our own.

The deepest form of romantic belonging does not require possession or fusion. It allows two independent people to belong to each other while remaining fully themselves. Similarly, parents who over-nurture their children risk having them grow up without knowing vital life skills and having mental health issues (Clarke et al. 2014; here).

The healthiest romantic love is therefore not necessarily about being loved less, but about being loved more adequately. Sometimes, what we really mean by love me less is: Love me without consuming me; love me without idealizing me; love me without making me your entire world; love me—and let me live more the way I want.

Love may be essential to a flourishing life, but love is not all we need.
